docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
PyRUA-Lean (Python for lean Robot-Use Agents, the robot counterpart of computer-use agents) turns a robot into a Python object. A tool-calling agent spends a full LLM call on every small step of a task and re-sends everything before it each time. A PyRUA-Lean agent writes code against robo instead, so one call can find an object, move above it, grasp, check the gripper and try again.

PyRUA-Lean has three parts so far:

  • The framework. The agent composes robot primitives, VLA policies among them, into Python cells that check and retry locally and return only the images and state it asks for. On 700 task instances from LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboCasa365, with the same GPT-6 Astra planner and the same primitives as tool calling, success goes from 63.1% to 71.7%, with 49% fewer LLM calls and 65% fewer input tokens on the instances both agents solve.
  • RoboDojo. With this library's own motion, gripper and perception primitives and the colour images of the benchmark's default observation, PyRUA-Lean reaches 51.62% average success rate (Score 58.20), first on all five dimensions of the public leaderboard (snapshot of October 9, 2026).
  • PyRUA-Lean Coder v0.1-4B. Qwen3.5-4B trained with GRPO in the PyRUA-Lean framework, on 45 LIBERO-PRO instances, goes from 18.8% to 44.1% on 655 task instances it never saw in training, above the Qwen3.5-27B base model (29.2%).

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/DAGroup-PKU/PyRUA-Lean.git && cd PyRUA-Lean
uv pip install -e .       # into the Python environment of your RPent robot stack (or pip)
pyrualean api             # the robot API the agent sees; no simulator needed

# one LIBERO-PRO episode: GPT-6 Astra writes code against robo, at most 40 code cells
export RPENT_ROOT=/path/to/rpent
pyrualean play --arm cells --suite libero_spatial_swap --task 7 --seed 2 \
    --model gpt-6-astra --max-turns 40 --budget-s 7200 --out runs/demo --cuda-device 0
pyrualean summarize runs/demo

LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboCasa365 run on RPent's robot stacks (the Quick Start sets one up step by step); RoboDojo runs through XPolicyLab and needs no RPent (RoboDojo).

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: A tool-calling agent spends a full LLM call on every small step of a task and re-sends everything before it each time. A PyRUA-Lean agent writes code against a robot object, robo, instead: one call can find an object, move above it, grasp, check the gripper and try again.

docs.title: What the agent gets
docs.text:
One tool, python(code), over a persistent namespace that holds robo (and np, math, time). Variables, functions and files the agent made stay there from one cell to the next. A second tool, finish, ends the episode. The code runs in a sandbox: a fixed set of imports, file access confined to its workspace, and no handle to the simulator behind robo.

This is one cell exactly as GPT-6 Astra wrote it in a LIBERO-PRO episode, placing a held bowl on a plate; the three comment lines are ours, and plate was located by an earlier cell:

# compose: compute a placement target from the scene geometry
held_at_plate = robo.segment(point=(314, 795))
print('bowl above plate', held_at_plate)
assert held_at_plate.found
correction = np.array(plate.world_xyz[:2]) - np.array(held_at_plate.world_xyz[:2])
place_xy = np.array(robo.state().eef_pos[:2]) + correction
surface_map = robo.world_map()
bowl_patch = surface_map[290:365, 740:850]
bowl_heights = bowl_patch[:,:,2]
bowl_heights = bowl_heights[(bowl_heights>1.04) & (bowl_heights<1.17)]
bottom_z = float(np.quantile(bowl_heights, 0.02))
placement_z = plate.world_xyz[2] + robo.state().eef_pos[2] - bottom_z + 0.007
print('correction', correction, 'bottom', bottom_z, 'placement z', placement_z)
assert np.linalg.norm(correction)<0.07 and 0.95<placement_z<1.05
# compose: lower, check, and release within the cell
lower = robo.move_to([*place_xy, placement_z], gripper=+1, step_clip=0.012, tol=0.005, max_steps=100)
print('lower', lower)
if lower.reached and not robo.done:
    print('release', robo.release())
print('done', robo.done)
# select: ask for an image only if the task is unfinished
if not robo.done:
    robo.show('agentview')

The cell printed five lines and asked for no image: the bowl was on the plate and the task was done. With tool calling, the same step took four LLM calls, and every move returned three camera images.

docs.title: What robo returns
docs.text:
• Results, not exceptions. A motion blocks until it is done and returns what actually happened (Move.reached, Pick.success, ...); a mask that was not found is a result too. Only misuse raises.
  • A finished episode stops everything. Once the benchmark's success check fires, robo.done is true and every further motion is refused. RoboDojo judges only the final scene: its robot has no done, and RoboDojo's client ends the episode itself when the task is solved.
  • Every call is recorded, with its arguments, its outcome and the simulator steps it took.

Each robot page lists that robot's primitives and the full API reference.

docs.title: What the model reads
docs.text:
1. The contract: what to do, how the code is run, how the episode is judged.
  2. The API reference of robo, generated from the robot class itself, so it cannot drift from the code (pyrualean api prints LIBERO-PRO's; each robot page shows its own).
  3. The robot's knowledge text: frames, units, how the primitives behave, what to watch out for. The same for every task; no task recipes.
  4. A task card: the instruction, the first camera images and the robot's starting state. Nothing privileged.

A play episode saves the whole prompt its model read as prompt.txt in the run directory; pyrualean prompt prints the prompt of a single shot (generate).

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Install PyRUA-Lean, run one LIBERO-PRO episode and look at what the agent did. In this example GPT-6 Astra writes the code through the Codex CLI, Pi0.5 does the grasping and SAM3 finds the objects.

For RoboDojo, follow RoboDojo instead: it runs through XPolicyLab and needs none of the RPent steps below.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Linux, an NVIDIA GPU and a CUDA 12 driver; EGL for headless rendering.
  • uv, git, and Node.js for the Codex CLI.
  • Access to the model: an account the Codex CLI can log in with, or an OpenAI Responses-compatible endpoint and its key. Model calls are billed by the provider.

Each RPent robot runs in its own RPent checkout and environment: their extras conflict, and RoboCasa365 needs Python 3.10.

docs.title: 1. Install RPent's LIBERO-PRO stack
docs.text:
LIBERO-PRO runs on RPent's stack, at the commit the paper used:

git clone https://github.com/RLinf/RPent.git && cd RPent && git checkout 886b3b2
uv venv --python 3.11 && source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install torch==2.7.1 torchvision==0.22.1 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
uv pip install -e ".[libero-pro]"
export RPENT_ROOT=$PWD
cd ..

docs.title: 2. Install PyRUA-Lean
docs.text:
Into the same environment:

git clone https://github.com/DAGroup-PKU/PyRUA-Lean.git
uv pip install -e ./PyRUA-Lean
pyrualean api             # the robot API the agent will see; no simulator needed

PyRUA-Lean declares no dependencies of its own: what it imports (numpy, Pillow and, for play, mcp 1.x, uvicorn and httpx) comes with RPent's environment.

docs.title: 3. Download Assets and Models
docs.text:
liberopro-download-assets --assets-dir /path/to/liberopro-assets
hf download RLinf/RLinf-Pi05-LIBERO-130-fullshot-SFT --exclude optimizer.pt --local-dir /path/to/pi05
hf auth login                                                     # facebook/sam3 is gated: accept its licence first
hf download facebook/sam3 sam3.pt --local-dir /path/to/sam3

export LIBERO_PRO_ASSET_PATH=/path/to/liberopro-assets
export PI05_CHECKPOINT_PATH=/path/to/pi05
export SAM3_CHECKPOINT_PATH=/path/to/sam3/sam3.pt
export LIBERO_TYPE=pro ROBOT_PLATFORM=LIBERO MUJOCO_GL=egl PYOPENGL_PLATFORM=egl XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false
export LIBERO_CONFIG_PATH=/path/to/a/writable/dir

liberopro looks for its assets inside its own package: replace site-packages/liberopro/liberopro/assets by a symlink to the assets directory. LIBERO-PRO has the details.

docs.title: 4. Configure the Agent
docs.text:
npm install -g @openai/codex@0.155.1
codex login                # or an endpoint: --base-url https://host/v1 --api-key-env MY_KEY

The Codex CLI speaks the OpenAI Responses API; a server that only serves chat completions (SGLang, vLLM) is used with --runtime openai instead. Agent Configuration covers the runtimes.

docs.title: 5. Run Your First Episode
docs.text:
Task 7 of libero_spatial_swap at seed 2, with at most 40 code cells and two hours:

pyrualean play --arm cells --suite libero_spatial_swap --task 7 --seed 2 \
    --model gpt-6-astra --max-turns 40 --budget-s 7200 --out runs/demo --cuda-device 0

Each episode boots its own simulator, Pi0.5 and SAM3 servers (about 100 s and 10 GB of GPU memory) unless it is attached to running ones (Running Episodes).

docs.title: 6. Look at the Result
docs.text:
pyrualean summarize runs/demo

runs/demo keeps the episode video, every cell the agent ran and what it printed, the primitives it called, the token usage and LIBERO's verdict (Output Files).

docs.title: Agent Configuration
docs.text:
Pick who runs the agent loop with one flag:

pyrualean play --runtime {codex,claude,openai} ...

Every runtime gets the same prompt, the same python (or run_program) and finish tools and the same budgets, and the episode is judged the same way. They differ in which product drives the conversation and what it adds: Codex keeps its own shell, sandboxed to the workspace; Claude Code its read-only Read, Glob and Grep; the openai loop adds nothing.

--runtime What it is When to pick it codex (default) The Codex CLI runs the loop; PyRUA-Lean serves it the tools. GPT models, with a Codex login or an OpenAI Responses endpoint. claude Claude Code, through the Claude Agent SDK. Claude models. openai A plain loop in PyRUA-Lean against any OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint: a gateway, or a local SGLang or vLLM server. Open models such as PyRUA-Lean Coder; RoboDojo.

--model names the model as the endpoint knows it. --reasoning sets the reasoning effort of Codex and Claude Code (default xhigh); with openai, put it in --openai-extra-body.

docs.title: Codex
docs.text:
npm install -g @openai/codex@0.155.1
  • Without further options the code arm uses whatever provider the Codex home is logged in to.
  • --base-url https://host/v1 --api-key-env MY_KEY sends it to an endpoint instead (the key is read from the variable MY_KEY). Codex speaks the Responses API there; a server that serves only chat completions needs --runtime openai.
  • For a run nothing else may leak into, give it a clean Codex home with --codex-home: a directory with only the credentials and a config.toml that sets approval_policy = "never" and memories = false under [features]. --codex-bin should point at the real Codex binary, not a wrapper.
  • Long episodes: with gpt-6-astra Codex assumes a 272k-token window and compacts the conversation at a threshold derived from it. The paper's runs set model_auto_compact_token_limit = 945000 in the Codex home's config.toml (or CODEX_AUTO_COMPACT_TOKEN_LIMIT=945000), so no episode was compacted; result.json records the setting (host.codex_context) and any compaction (generation.compactions).

GPT-6 Astra on Codex 0.155.1

Codex 0.155.1 runs gpt-6-astra in "code mode", which hides every tool behind one JavaScript tool. PyRUA-Lean passes Codex a model catalog that turns this off (direct function calls, as in the paper's runs), so nothing needs to be done for play and generate.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
pip install claude-agent-sdk          # into the robot stack's environment
pyrualean play --runtime claude --model <claude model> --claude-cli /path/to/claude ...

Claude Code reaches the model the way it is configured to (ANTHROPIC_* variables). Opus 5.5 needs Claude Code 2.1.280 or newer. --reasoning none turns thinking off.

docs.title: OpenAI-compatible endpoints
docs.text:
pyrualean play --runtime openai --base-url http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1 --api-key-env MY_KEY \
    --model <model name> ...

Without --base-url and --api-key-env, the loop reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY.

Option Meaning (default) --openai-max-tokens the longest reply (4096) --openai-extra-body JSON merged into every request, e.g. {"reasoning_effort": "high"} --openai-nudges replies without a tool call tolerated before the episode ends (2) --openai-tool-choice auto or required (auto) --openai-temperature, --openai-timeout-s sampling temperature, request timeout (900 s) --image-max-side downscale images to this longest side (0: keep)

A rate-limited endpoint (HTTP 429) is waited out, not counted as a failure.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command What it does pyrualean api Print the API reference the agent reads (LIBERO-PRO's robot). --primitives no-vla leaves the VLA out. pyrualean prompt Print the prompt of a single shot (generate); --card renders it for a task card. A play episode saves the prompt its model read as prompt.txt in the run directory. pyrualean play Run one episode with an agent (Running Episodes). pyrualean card Boot only the simulator and save a task card. pyrualean generate Ask the model for a whole program from a task card (single shot). pyrualean run Run a program file for one episode. pyrualean summarize Tabulate run directories (Output Files).

docs.title: The task instance
docs.text:
play, card and run take the same options:

Option Meaning (default) --robot libero, robotwin or robocasa (libero). play also takes robodojo_xpl_rgb, which starts RoboDojo's own client itself (it needs ROBODOJO_SOURCE_ROOT and one environment with both sides); RoboDojo's official evaluation runs through XPolicyLab (RoboDojo) --suite LIBERO suite, RoboTwin task config or RoboCasa split --task LIBERO task index, or the robot's task name --seed the scene seed (0; always pass it, since the robots' own defaults are not used) --out the run directory --cuda-device the GPU the episode's servers use --max-episode-steps the simulator step limit (10000) --rpent-root, --python the RPent checkout and the interpreter it is installed in

docs.title: play
docs.text: Option Meaning (default) --arm cells or program --runtime codex, claude or openai (codex; Agent Configuration) --model, --reasoning the model (gpt-6-astra) and its reasoning effort (xhigh) --base-url, --api-key-env an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and the variable holding its key --max-turns the decision budget, in code cells --budget-s the wall-clock budget, in seconds (1200) --images on-motion, on-demand or none (on-motion) --feedback rich or pure (rich) --primitives full or no-vla (full) --max-programs the most programs on the program arm --guides, --guides-dir operating guides in the agent's workspace --vla-endpoint, --sam3-endpoint running model servers to attach to --codex-home, --codex-bin, --claude-cli the runtimes' homes and executables

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Variable Meaning RPENT_ROOT the RPent checkout, when RPent is not installed as a package PYRUALEAN_RUNTIME default of --runtime PYRUALEAN_PRIMITIVES default of --primitives PYRUALEAN_CODEX_BIN, PYRUALEAN_CODEX_HOME defaults of --codex-bin, --codex-home PYRUALEAN_CLAUDE_CLI default of --claude-cli PYRUALEAN_OPENAI_EXTRA_BODY default of --openai-extra-body PYRUALEAN_CODEX_RETRIES retries of a request from Codex (play, generate) to a --base-url endpoint (10) OPENAI_BASE_URL, OPENAI_API_KEY the endpoint and key of --runtime openai when --base-url / --api-key-env are not given PYRUALEAN_OPENAI_RETRIES, PYRUALEAN_OPENAI_TIMEOUT_S retries (10) and request timeout in seconds (900) of --runtime openai CODEX_AUTO_COMPACT_TOKEN_LIMIT Codex's compaction threshold for the episode (Agent Configuration)

pyrualean play passes --runtime and --primitives on only when they differ from codex and full, so a PYRUALEAN_RUNTIME or PYRUALEAN_PRIMITIVES in the environment also wins over an explicit --runtime codex or --primitives full: unset it to get those.

Each robot page lists the variables of its stack: checkpoints, assets and rendering.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
pip install -e '.[dev]'
pytest          # offline tests against scripted backends
ruff check .

docs.title: Output Files
docs.text:
Every episode writes one run directory (--out).

File What it holds result.json The verdict (environment_success), the arm, how the agent finished, token usage and LLM calls, and the settings of the run. episode.mp4 The episode video (RPent robots; on RoboDojo the run directory keeps each step's images under steps/, and RoboDojo records the videos). workspace/ Every cell or program the agent ran, and the files it wrote. tool_turns.json Each tool call: which tool, how long it took, whether it moved the robot, the simulator steps, and anything the sandbox flagged. calls.jsonl Every primitive call: arguments, outcome, wall time and simulator steps. prompt.txt, card.json, card/*.png The prompt and the task card the model received. codex_events.jsonl / claude_events.jsonl / openai_events.jsonl The runtime's own record of the conversation (with --runtime openai, also messages.json). states.json, per-step images The robot stack's own records (RPent robots). policy.py, policy_output.txt The program and what it printed (single shot). host.log The log of the robot host that ran the episode: where to look when play reports that it failed.

On RoboDojo, RoboDojo's evaluation client keeps its own records as well (RoboDojo).

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
pyrualean summarize runs/demo runs/other           # one row per episode
pyrualean summarize --json runs/demo runs/other    # the same rows, then the totals as JSON: success rate, statuses, mean calls and tokens

Give summarize run directories, not a folder that also holds other things.

A crash, a timeout or an episode that did not boot counts as a failed episode.

docs.title: Running Episodes
docs.text:
pyrualean play runs one episode: it boots the robot, gives the agent the task and serves its code until the episode is over.

pyrualean play --arm cells --suite libero_spatial_swap --task 7 --seed 2 \
    --model gpt-6-astra --max-turns 40 --budget-s 7200 --out runs/demo --cuda-device 0

--robot picks the robot (libero, the default, robotwin or robocasa) and --suite, --task, --seed the task instance; each robot page says what they mean there. Always pass --seed: play sends 0 when it is left out, whatever the robot's own default. RoboDojo runs through XPolicyLab (RoboDojo).

docs.title: Cells or programs
docs.text:
--arm What one LLM call runs What carries over cells a cell in a persistent namespace with robo, like a notebook variables, functions, imports, files program a complete program, def run(robo): ..., in a fresh namespace files in the workspace, and the conversation

--max-programs N caps the number of programs on the program arm; 1 is a single shot whose result the agent still sees.

docs.title: What the agent sees after a call
docs.text: Option Values --images on-motion (default): the current camera images after every call that moved the robot. on-demand: an image only when the code asked for one with robo.show(camera). none. --feedback rich (default): what the code printed, plus the robot's state and the primitives it called. pure: only what the code printed.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.text: Option Meaning --max-turns N A decision budget: at most N code cells (python or run_program calls; finish is not counted). The agent knows the cells are limited, not how many. --budget-s S A wall-clock budget in seconds, thinking included (default 1200). With --max-turns it is a safety ceiling: set it well above what the cells take, so that outcomes do not depend on how fast the provider is (the paper's runs used 7200).

docs.title: VLA policies, guides and shared servers
docs.text:
• --primitives no-vla removes the robot's VLA primitives: they disappear from the API reference and the knowledge text, and calling one is refused.
  • --guides gives the agent RPent's three LIBERO operating guides in its workspace (optional reading); --guides-dir <dir> gives it the *.md files of another directory.
  • --vla-endpoint host:port (and --sam3-endpoint on LIBERO-PRO) attach the episode to running model servers instead of booting its own; the simulator is always the episode's own.

docs.title: A single shot
docs.text:
The strictest setting: one reply, one program, no feedback.

pyrualean card --suite libero_object_swap --task 2 --seed 0 --out runs/card --cuda-device 0
pyrualean generate --card runs/card/card.json --out runs/gen --model gpt-6-astra
pyrualean run --policy runs/gen/policy.py --suite libero_object_swap --task 2 --seed 0 \
    --out runs/code --cuda-device 0

card boots only the simulator and saves the task card; generate asks the model for policy.py (--transfer tells it the program will run on other seeds, so it must not rely on pixels); run runs the file once, with a hard timeout, and a crash or timeout counts as a failed episode.

docs.title: PyRUA-Lean Coder v0.1-4B
docs.text:
DAGroup-PKU/PyRUA-Lean-Coder-v0.1-4B

PyRUA-Lean Coder v0.1-4B is Qwen3.5-4B trained with GRPO in the PyRUA-Lean framework, on 45 LIBERO-PRO task instances, as its planner: it writes the cells, the primitives do the rest. On 655 task instances it never saw in training it goes from 18.8% to 44.1%, above the Qwen3.5-27B base model (29.2%).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Success rate (%), PyRUA-Lean framework:

Planner Trained on (45) LIBERO-PRO other (155) RoboTwin 2.0 (250) RC365 atomic (90) RC365 composite (160) All unseen (655) Qwen3.5-4B 37.8 13.5 14.0 52.2 12.5 18.8 Qwen3.5-27B 64.4 38.1 20.8 65.6 13.1 29.2 PyRUA-Lean Coder v0.1-4B 71.1 37.4 52.4 76.7 19.4 44.1

RoboTwin 2.0 and both RoboCasa365 sets are benchmarks it was not trained on at all; the LIBERO-PRO column of the unseen part holds that benchmark's other tasks.

docs.title: Running the model
docs.text:
An open model runs behind any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (a local SGLang or vLLM server, for example) and is driven by the in-process loop of pyrualean play --runtime openai (Agent Configuration). With SGLang:

python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path DAGroup-PKU/PyRUA-Lean-Coder-v0.1-4B --port 30000 \
    --context-length 65536 --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
    --constrained-json-disable-any-whitespace

Then one LIBERO-PRO episode, on a task the model never saw in training (RPent's LIBERO-PRO stack installed as the Quick Start describes):

export RPENT_ROOT=/path/to/rpent OPENAI_API_KEY=none
pyrualean play --robot libero --arm cells --suite libero_goal_swap --task 3 --seed 0 \
    --runtime openai --base-url http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1 --api-key-env OPENAI_API_KEY \
    --model DAGroup-PKU/PyRUA-Lean-Coder-v0.1-4B \
    --openai-max-tokens 8192 --openai-tool-choice required --openai-temperature 1.0 \
    --openai-extra-body '{"top_p": 0.95, "top_k": 20}' \
    --images on-demand --feedback pure --guides --max-turns 40 --budget-s 5400 \
    --out runs/coder-demo --cuda-device 0
pyrualean summarize runs/coder-demo

These are the settings of the paper's evaluation: a reply of at most 8,192 tokens, a context of 65,536 tokens (an episode that outgrows it ends there), at most 40 code cells and 90 minutes.

docs.title: Robots
docs.text:
Robot Benchmark Runs on VLA policy Cameras the agent sees robodojo_xpl_rgb RoboDojo XPolicyLab, under RoboDojo's own evaluation client none (SAM3 for segmentation) three colour cameras libero (default) LIBERO-PRO RPent Pi0.5 (and SAM3) agentview, wrist robotwin RoboTwin 2.0 RPent LingBot-VLA head, two wrists robocasa RoboCasa365 RPent RLDX-1 agentview, navview, wrist

New robots are added through XPolicyLab (Adding a Robot): the benchmark's own client runs the simulator and judges the episode, and one adapter directory can serve the benchmarks XPolicyLab integrates (today: RoboDojo). LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboCasa365 run on RPent's stacks.

Every robot page gives the API reference the agent reads, generated from the robot class when these docs are built.

docs.title: Adding a Robot
docs.text: Robots are added through XPolicyLab. The benchmark's own evaluation client keeps the simulator, the observation and the verdict; PyRUA-Lean answers it as a policy, through the adapter that every benchmark XPolicyLab integrates already talks to. RoboDojo is the reference implementation.

docs.title: How an episode runs
docs.text:
1. The client sends an observation (update_obs). On the first one of a trial, the adapter starts a PyRUA-Lean episode: the agent loop, the sandboxed cells and the robot robo.
  2. A cell calls a primitive; the primitive turns what it was asked into native actions, computed from the observation.
  3. The client asks for an action (get_action) and gets the next one. While the model is still thinking, the answer is "wait" and the adapter asks again, so the client's request never times out.
  4. The client steps the simulator and sends the observation that followed, which the primitive reads to report what happened.
  5. When the episode is over (the task solved, the action budget spent, or the program finished), the client reports the verdict (trial_end).

pyrualean.hosts.xpolicylab_bridge turns XPolicyLab's two calls into an environment a primitive can step; it is the same for every robot.

docs.title: What a robot needs
docs.text:
Piece File RoboDojo Robot class: the API the agent writes against, one method per primitive with typed results; its docstrings are the API reference in the prompt src/pyrualean/<robot>.py robodojo.py (RobodojoRobot), specialised by robodojo_xpl_rgb.py Primitives: motion, gripper and perception of this library's own, computed from the observation src/pyrualean/hosts/<robot>_tools.py and helpers robodojo_tools.py, robodojo_kinematics.py, robodojo_sight.py Toolkit: the primitives over an environment that has only an observation and an action, with each step's images and state recorded src/pyrualean/hosts/<robot>_native.py robodojo_native.py Host: builds the toolkit over the bridge and writes the task card; for pyrualean play on one machine it also starts the benchmark's client src/pyrualean/hosts/xpolicylab_<benchmark>.py xpolicylab_robodojo.py, xpolicylab_robodojo_rgb.py Knowledge: one text for every task src/pyrualean/knowledge/<robot>.md, <robot>-novla.md robodojo_xpl_rgb.md, robodojo_xpl_rgb-novla.md Adapter: XPolicyLab's policy directory integrations/xpolicylab/PyRUA_Lean/ the same directory

Shared, and not changed by a new robot: the bridge, the agent runtimes (Agent Configuration), the cells and their sandbox, and the prompt with its API reference generated from the robot class.

docs.title: The robot class
docs.text:
• Every public method and property is rendered into the API reference from its signature and docstring, so write them for the model; everything host-facing starts with _.
  • Results, not exceptions: what a primitive measured (reached, found, how wide the gripper is) is a field of a frozen result dataclass. ValueError for bad arguments, ToolError when a tool fails, EpisodeFinished once the episode is over.
  • A member the benchmark cannot support goes into ABSENT_MEMBERS instead of answering with a constant: RoboDojo judges only the final scene, so its robot has no done.
  • Only what a program cannot compose from other primitives is a primitive; the knowledge text says how to compose the rest (on RoboDojo a twist is a move_to with another roll, a button press a move_to past the surface).
  • Nothing privileged: the primitives read the observation the client sends, and constants of the embodiment and the default scene taken from the benchmark's public configuration.
  • The class subclasses RobotBase (src/pyrualean/_robot.py): it declares CAMERAS, IMAGE_ARTIFACTS, ON_MOTION_IMAGES, STATEFUL_TOOLS, RESULT_TYPES and VLA_PRIMITIVES, implements _state_from_envelope and _summary_dict, and sends every primitive through _readonly or _stateful.
  • The module ends with its registration, ADAPTER = RobotAdapter(name=..., robot_cls=..., host=..., knowledge=..., blurb=...), with the XPolicyLab host as host, and the robot's name goes into ROBOTS in src/pyrualean/robots.py: get_adapter refuses any other name.

docs.title: The adapter
docs.text:
integrations/xpolicylab/PyRUA_Lean/ is one directory for every benchmark, as XPolicyLab keeps one per policy.

File Role deploy.yml The robot, the primitive set, the runtime, the model, the budgets, when the model sees images and what a tool call returns. model.py XPolicyLab's model: starts one PyRUA-Lean episode per trial on the first observation and serves it through the bridge. It knows RoboDojo today; a new benchmark adds its robot and host here, chosen by bench_name. deploy.py XPolicyLab's evaluation loop with three changes for a policy that thinks between actions: ask again on "wait", end the episode on an empty answer, and pass the step count and limit with every observation. It reports the verdict back through trial_end. eval.sh, setup_eval_policy_server.sh, setup_eval_env_client.sh XPolicyLab's entry scripts. install.sh, download_assets.sh The policy environment and SAM3's checkpoint. README.md XPolicyLab's policy README: installation, evaluation, configuration and notes.

docs.title: The knowledge text
docs.text: knowledge/<robot>.md (and <robot>-novla.md without the VLA primitives) is the same for every task: frames and units, how each primitive behaves, how to judge progress from the images, and the benchmark's success rules that an instruction does not spell out (RoboDojo, for most tasks: both arms back at their start pose, the grippers open). No task recipes.

docs.title: Checking a new robot
docs.text:
1. Unit tests against a scripted environment, for every primitive and the API reference (tests/test_robodojo*.py).
  2. XPolicyLab's debug client, which exercises the loop, the action keys and their dimensions without a simulator or a model: EVAL_ENV_TYPE=debug bash eval.sh <bench_name> <task> ....
  3. One episode with pyrualean play --robot <robot>, which starts the benchmark's client itself (for RoboDojo it needs ROBODOJO_SOURCE_ROOT and one environment with both sides).
  4. A few episodes with a model through the benchmark's official entry (RoboDojo: scripts/robodojo.sh eval), then the full task set.

docs.title: LIBERO-PRO
docs.text:
Runs on RPent

LIBERO-PRO runs on RPent's LIBERO stack: RPent boots the simulator, the Pi0.5 VLA and SAM3, and every robo call goes through RPent's toolkit. New robots are added through XPolicyLab (Adding a Robot).

LIBERO-PRO perturbs LIBERO's tabletop tasks: swapped objects and positions, rephrased or changed instructions. The robot is a simulated Franka arm with RPent's scripted servos, the frozen Pi0.5 VLA skills and SAM3 perception.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Robot Franka arm in MuJoCo / robosuite Action models Pi0.5 (pi0_pick, pi0_doubled); SAM3 for segmentation Agent runtimes codex (default), claude, openai (Agent Configuration) Tasks The LIBERO-PRO suites RPent runs, e.g. libero_object_swap, libero_spatial_swap Hardware Linux, NVIDIA GPU, EGL; Python 3.11

docs.title: Observation and Action
docs.text: Item Description Observation The agentview and wrist images, their per-pixel world coordinates, the end-effector pose, the gripper opening and the scene's object names. Action The agent's cells call robo; each call is one RPent tool (a scripted servo or a Pi0.5 skill) that steps the simulator. Success LIBERO's own task predicate. robo.done turns true once it fires, and every further motion is refused. Task prompt The suite's task instruction, a task card (the step-0 images and the initial gripper pose) and the robot's knowledge text.

docs.title: Installation and Resources
docs.text:
RPent at commit 886b3b2, in its own Python 3.11 environment, with PyRUA-Lean in the same environment:

git clone https://github.com/RLinf/RPent.git && cd RPent && git checkout 886b3b2
uv venv --python 3.11 && source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install torch==2.7.1 torchvision==0.22.1 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
uv pip install -e ".[libero-pro]"
uv pip install -e /path/to/PyRUA-Lean
liberopro-download-assets --assets-dir /path/to/liberopro-assets

liberopro looks for its assets inside its own package: replace site-packages/liberopro/liberopro/assets by a symlink to the assets directory. Then the environment:

export LIBERO_PRO_ASSET_PATH=/path/to/liberopro-assets
export LIBERO_TYPE=pro ROBOT_PLATFORM=LIBERO MUJOCO_GL=egl PYOPENGL_PLATFORM=egl XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false
export LIBERO_CONFIG_PATH=/path/to/a/writable/dir
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=4 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=4 MKL_NUM_THREADS=4      # as in the paper's runs

docs.title: VLA Configuration
docs.text:
Pi0.5 RLinf/RLinf-Pi05-LIBERO-130-fullshot-SFT from Hugging Face (optimizer.pt is not needed):

hf download RLinf/RLinf-Pi05-LIBERO-130-fullshot-SFT --local-dir /path/to/pi05
export PI05_CHECKPOINT_PATH=/path/to/pi05

docs.title: SAM3 Configuration
docs.text:
hf auth login                                                     # facebook/sam3 is gated: accept its licence first
hf download facebook/sam3 sam3.pt --local-dir /path/to/sam3
export SAM3_CHECKPOINT_PATH=/path/to/sam3/sam3.pt

docs.title: Task Selection
docs.text: Option Meaning --suite A LIBERO-PRO suite, e.g. libero_object_swap. --task Zero-based task index within the suite. --seed Environment seed (default 0). --libero-type The installed LIBERO variant (default pro).

docs.title: Run a Task
docs.text:
export RPENT_ROOT=/path/to/rpent
pyrualean play --arm cells --suite libero_spatial_swap --task 7 --seed 2 \
    --model gpt-6-astra --max-turns 40 --budget-s 7200 --out runs/demo --cuda-device 0
pyrualean summarize runs/demo

An episode with private servers boots Pi0.5 and SAM3 (~10 GB of GPU memory, ~100 s); attached to running servers (--vla-endpoint / --sam3-endpoint) it needs ~1.5 GB and ~15 s. --guides gives the agent RPent's three LIBERO operating guides (Running Episodes).

docs.title: View Results
docs.text: The run directory keeps the episode video (episode.mp4), every cell the agent ran (workspace/) and what each printed (the runtime's event file, e.g. codex_events.jsonl), the ledger of primitive calls (calls.jsonl), the token usage and LIBERO's verdict (result.json), and RPent's own records (states.json, per-step images).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
GPT-6 Astra, 40 tasks at five seeds (200 task instances), at most 40 LLM calls and two hours per episode. Against RPent's tool-calling agent with the same planner and primitives; LLM calls, input tokens and cost per solved episode on the instances both solved:

Success (%) LLM calls Input tokens Cost Tool calling (RPent) 83.0 21.4 1.23M $2.49 PyRUA-Lean 94.0 8.4 273k $0.79

docs.title: What Runs Where
docs.text:
• Env server (RPent) owns the LIBERO MuJoCo environment and its EGL rendering.
  • Pi0.5 server and SAM3 server (RPent) hold the VLA and the segmentation model.
  • PyRUA-Lean boots them for the episode, builds RPent's toolkit and serves the agent's cells against robo.
  • Agent runtime (Codex CLI, Claude Code or the openai loop) talks to the model.

docs.title: Primitives the Agent Can Call
docs.text:
Motion:

  • move_to(xyz, gripper, ...): servo the gripper to a world position, holding its orientation.
  • move_pose(xyz, target_pitch=..., target_yaw=..., ...): servo position and wrist orientation together.
  • rotate_wrist(target_yaw= / delta_yaw=), rotate_pitch(target_pitch= / delta_pitch=): turn or tilt the gripper.
  • set_gripper(gripper, steps), release(): drive the gripper; open it and let go.
  • pi0_pick(prompt): let the frozen Pi0.5 VLA perform a closed-loop grasp.
  • pi0_doubled(prompt): let Pi0.5 perform a contact skill that is not a pick.

Perception and state:

  • segment(prompt | point=...): locate an object with SAM3 and return its world position.
  • back_project(row, col), region_center(row_range, col_range): the world point under a pixel, the centre of a pixel window.
  • state(), image(camera), world_map(camera), show(camera), camera_meta(camera), artifact(name), done.

How It Works gives the rules every call follows.

API reference: what the agent reads, generated from pyrualean.libero when these docs are built 
class LiberoRobot
    A LIBERO tabletop Franka arm with a two-finger gripper.

    World frame: x/y span the table, z is up, units are metres and radians.
    The arm starts at a home pose above the table, gripper open and pointing
    down.  Motion calls block until the primitive finishes and return a typed
    result describing what actually happened; nothing is queued.

    Gripper commands are floats: ``LiberoRobot.OPEN`` (-1) opens,
    ``LiberoRobot.CLOSE`` (+1) closes and keeps holding.  Every motion call
    takes a ``gripper`` argument that is *held for the whole motion*; carrying
    an object with the default ``gripper=-1`` silently drops it.

    Perception is camera based: the scene is observed through a fixed
    ``agentview`` camera (global layout) and a ``wrist`` camera (close range).
    Object poses are never given; use ``segment`` / ``back_project`` on the
    recorded images to obtain world coordinates.

Constants:
    robo.OPEN = -1.0
    robo.CLOSE = 1.0

Methods and attributes of `robo`:

robo.task -> str  (read-only attribute)
    The task instruction, e.g. ``"put the bowl on the plate"``.

robo.done -> bool  (read-only attribute)
    True once the benchmark's success predicate has fired (sticky).

robo.state(step: int = -1) -> State
    Read the recorded proprioceptive state.

    Args:
        step: recorded step to read; ``-1`` is the latest, ``0`` the
            initial scene.  A new step is recorded after every motion call.
    Returns:
        State with gripper position, orientation, finger opening, the
        object names and the episode flags.

robo.image(
    camera: str = 'agentview',
    *,
    resolution: str = 'high',
    step: int = -1,
) -> Any
    Load a recorded camera image as a ``numpy`` uint8 array (H, W, 3), RGB.

    Args:
        camera: ``"agentview"`` (fixed global view, best for identifying
            objects and layout) or ``"wrist"`` (camera on the gripper,
            best for close-range geometry).
        resolution: ``"high"`` (1024x1024) or ``"low"`` (256x256).  Pixel
            coordinates are (row, col) with row 0 at the top and col 0 at
            the left; pass the same resolution to ``back_project``.
        step: recorded step, ``-1`` = latest.

robo.world_map(
    camera: str = 'agentview',
    *,
    resolution: str = 'high',
    step: int = -1,
) -> Any
    Load the per-pixel world coordinates of a recorded image.

    Returns a ``numpy`` float array (H, W, 3): ``world_map[row, col]`` is
    the [x, y, z] of the surface seen at that pixel (zeros / non-finite
    where depth is invalid).  This is what ``back_project`` reads; load it
    when you want to reason about many pixels at once.

robo.show(camera: str = 'agentview') -> None
    Attach the current image of ``camera`` to the feedback of this turn.

    Images are not returned automatically; call ``show("agentview")`` or
    ``show("wrist")`` when *you* (the author) need to look at the scene
    before writing the next turn.  Costs tokens: look only when a
    decision depends on it.

robo.artifact(name: str, *, step: int = -1) -> bytes
    Return the raw bytes of a recorded artifact (advanced).

    Names include ``agentview_high.png``, ``wrist_high.png``,
    ``agentview_depth.npz`` and the ``overlay_artifact`` of a ``segment``.

robo.camera_meta(camera: str = 'agentview', *, step: int = -1) -> dict[str, Any]
    Return the camera calibration metadata (intrinsics/extrinsics) as a dict.

robo.segment(
    prompt: str | None = None,
    *,
    camera: str = 'agentview',
    point: tuple[int, int] | None = None,
    min_score: float = 0.2,
    step: int = -1,
) -> Segment
    Locate an object with SAM3 on a recorded image and return its world position.

    Give exactly one of ``prompt`` (a short visual description) or
    ``point`` (a positive pixel ``(row, col)`` in the high-resolution
    image).  The top-ranked mask is projected through the world map, so
    ``world_xyz`` is the object's visible *surface* median: use its x/y for
    a target and pick z from the object's resting height.

    Args:
        prompt: colour + shape + relation, e.g. ``"the black bowl on the
            stove"``.  Brand or internal names (``"akita"``,
            ``"alphabet soup"``) score badly; describe what it looks like.
        camera: ``"agentview"`` for global identity, ``"wrist"`` for
            refinement once the gripper is 15-20 cm above the target.
        point: alternative to ``prompt``; a pixel on the object.
        min_score: reject masks below this confidence.
        step: recorded step whose image to use (``-1`` = latest).
    Returns:
        Segment; check ``found`` before using ``world_xyz``.

robo.back_project(
    row: int,
    col: int,
    *,
    camera: str = 'agentview',
    resolution: str = 'high',
    step: int = -1,
) -> BackProjection
    Return the world [x, y, z] of the surface seen at pixel ``(row, col)``.

    The pixel must come from the same camera and resolution as requested
    (``image(camera, resolution=...)``).  Sample several pixels firmly on
    an object's top surface and take the median; pixels on thin rims,
    edges or the gap to the table hit the background metres away.

    Raises:
        ToolError: pixel out of bounds or no valid depth at that pixel.

robo.region_center(
    row_range: tuple[int, int],
    col_range: tuple[int, int],
    *,
    camera: str = 'agentview',
    resolution: str = 'high',
    z_min: float | None = None,
    z_max: float | None = None,
    step: int = -1,
) -> RegionCenter
    Return the world centre of a pixel window (e.g. a container cavity).

    Uses the midpoint of the window's world x/y extent rather than a
    median, which is biased towards a rim or edge.  ``z_min`` / ``z_max``
    keep only pixels inside a world-z band (e.g. the basket floor).

    Raises:
        ToolError: empty window or too few valid pixels.

robo.move_to(
    xyz: list[float],
    gripper: float = -1.0,
    *,
    tol: float = 0.012,
    step_clip: float = 0.025,
    max_steps: int = 80,
    target_yaw: float | None = None,
    yaw_step_clip: float = 0.1,
    action_scale: float = 0.05,
) -> Move
    Servo the gripper to a world-frame position, holding its orientation.

    Args:
        xyz: target [x, y, z] in metres.  One call may move at most
            0.30 m in the x/y plane; longer traversals raise ValueError -
            split them into 2-3 waypoints at carrying height.
        gripper: -1 open, +1 close; held during the whole motion.
        tol: stop when within this distance (m).
        step_clip: per-step travel cap (m): 0.025 empty/box, 0.015 cans,
            0.012 tall bottles or fine approaches.
        max_steps: simulator step budget.
        target_yaw: optional world yaw (rad) to servo simultaneously.
        yaw_step_clip: per-step yaw cap (rad) when ``target_yaw`` is set.
        action_scale: OSC action scale; leave at the default.
    Returns:
        Move; check ``reached`` - a stalled servo returns normally.

robo.move_pose(
    xyz: list[float],
    *,
    target_pitch: float | None = None,
    target_yaw: float | None = None,
    gripper: float = -1.0,
    step_clip: float = 0.02,
    pitch_step: float = 0.08,
    yaw_step: float = 0.08,
    tol: float = 0.012,
    ori_tol: float = 0.05,
    max_steps: int = 150,
    action_scale: float = 0.05,
) -> MovePose
    Servo position and wrist orientation (pitch/yaw) at the same time.

    Use it where ``move_to`` stalls short of a low or recessed target
    (cabinet fronts, microwave cavities): co-varying tilt and position
    threads the IK singularity that a fixed gripper-down servo hits.
    ``gripper`` defaults to open; pass ``+1`` when holding an object.

robo.rotate_wrist(
    *,
    target_yaw: float | None = None,
    delta_yaw: float | None = None,
    gripper: float = 1.0,
    max_steps: int = 40,
    tol: float = 0.02,
    step_clip: float = 0.1,
) -> Rotation
    Rotate the gripper about the world z axis, keeping its position.

    Give exactly one of ``target_yaw`` (absolute, rad) or ``delta_yaw``
    (relative, rad).  ``state().eef_yaw`` reports the current yaw.
    ``gripper`` defaults to +1 (keep holding).

robo.rotate_pitch(
    *,
    target_pitch: float | None = None,
    delta_pitch: float | None = None,
    gripper: float = 1.0,
    max_steps: int = 40,
    tol: float = 0.02,
    step_clip: float = 0.1,
) -> Rotation
    Tilt the gripper about the world x axis, keeping position and yaw.

    Pitch 0 points the gripper straight down; +pi/2 points it along world
    +y, -pi/2 along -y.  Use before threading into an opening whose front
    faces along y.  Give exactly one of ``target_pitch`` or ``delta_pitch``.

robo.set_gripper(gripper: float, steps: int = 5) -> Gripper
    Hold the current pose and drive the gripper for ``steps`` simulator steps.

    ``set_gripper(+1, steps=8)`` right after a successful pick firms the
    grip before carrying (use ``steps<=5`` for a laterally weak can).

robo.release(max_steps: int = 20) -> Release
    Open the gripper in place for up to ``max_steps`` steps and let go.

    Returns as soon as the task predicate fires (``terminated``), so a
    successful placement usually ends the episode here.

robo.pi0_pick(
    prompt: str,
    *,
    max_chunks: int = 24,
    lift_thresh: float = 0.05,
    gripper_closed_thresh: float = 0.06,
    gripper_open_thresh: float = 0.0,
    descent_thresh: float = 0.1,
) -> Pick
    Let the frozen Pi0.5 VLA perform a closed-loop grasp.

    The VLA runs ``prompt`` for up to ``max_chunks`` action chunks (each a
    short burst of steps) and stops early once the gripper has descended by
    ``descent_thresh``, closed on something (opening in
    ``[gripper_open_thresh, gripper_closed_thresh)``) and risen by
    ``lift_thresh``.  Use it for the grasp: pre-position the gripper above
    the target, keep the prompt short (``"pick up the red mug"``), use a
    modest chunk budget (20 is the usual choice) and verify the grasp from
    the lift, the gripper closure and the images; then script the carry
    and release yourself.

    Returns:
        Pick; ``success`` is a heuristic - verify with ``state()`` and the
        wrist image before carrying.

robo.pi0_doubled(prompt: str, *, max_chunks: int = 20) -> Contact
    Let the frozen Pi0.5 VLA perform a contact skill that is not a pick.

    For knobs, buttons, drawers, doors and short pushes (``"turn on the
    stove"``, ``"open the top drawer"``).  Runs up to ``max_chunks`` chunks
    or until the task predicate fires.  ``success`` only mirrors that
    predicate; check the state or an image to judge an intermediate step.

Result types (frozen dataclasses; access fields as attributes):

class State(
    step: int,
    task: str,
    eef_pos: tuple[float, float, float],
    eef_quat: tuple[float, float, float, float],
    gripper_qpos: tuple[float, float],
    gripper_opening: float,
    object_names: tuple[str, ...],
    terminated: bool,
    truncated: bool,
)
    Proprioceptive snapshot of the robot at one recorded step.

    step: index of the recorded step (0 = initial scene).
    task: the task instruction given by the benchmark (authoritative).
    eef_pos: end-effector (gripper) position [x, y, z] in the world frame, metres.
    eef_quat: end-effector orientation quaternion [x, y, z, w].
    gripper_qpos: the two finger joint positions.
    gripper_opening: finger separation proxy, |q0| + |q1|.  About 0.08 when
        fully open, about 0.0 when closed on nothing; roughly 0.01-0.05 means
        the fingers closed on an object.
    object_names: names of the movable objects in the scene (no poses).
    terminated: the benchmark's success predicate has fired.
    truncated: the simulator step budget is exhausted.
    .eef_yaw -> float: World-frame yaw of the gripper in radians (as used by rotate_wrist).
    .eef_pitch -> float: Gripper tilt in radians (0 = pointing straight down; see rotate_pitch).

class Move(
    target_xyz: tuple[float, float, float],
    final_eef_pos: tuple[float, float, float],
    final_dist_m: float,
    reached: bool,
    steps_used: int,
    max_steps: int,
    terminated: bool,
    truncated: bool,
)
    Outcome of ``move_to``.

    target_xyz: the commanded target.
    final_eef_pos: where the gripper actually stopped.
    final_dist_m: distance between the two, metres.
    reached: ``final_dist_m <= tol``.  False means the servo stalled (IK limit,
        collision, or step budget) - re-plan instead of assuming you arrived.
    steps_used / max_steps: simulator steps consumed / allowed.
    terminated / truncated: episode flags after the move.

class MovePose(
    final_eef_pos: tuple[float, float, float],
    final_dist_m: float,
    final_pitch: float,
    reached: bool,
    steps_used: int,
    terminated: bool,
    truncated: bool,
)
    Outcome of ``move_pose`` (position and orientation servo).

    reached: position within ``tol`` (orientation errors are not folded in).
    final_pitch: gripper pitch after the move, radians.

class Rotation(
    start: float,
    target: float,
    final: float,
    final_err: float,
    reached: bool,
    steps_used: int,
    terminated: bool,
    truncated: bool,
)
    Outcome of ``rotate_wrist`` / ``rotate_pitch``; angles in radians.

    reached: ``abs(final_err) <= tol``.

class Gripper(gripper: float, steps: int, terminated: bool, truncated: bool)
    Outcome of ``set_gripper``: the command that was held and for how long.

class Release(
    steps_used: int,
    start_gripper_opening: float,
    peak_gripper_opening: float,
    final_gripper_opening: float,
    terminated: bool,
    truncated: bool,
)
    Outcome of ``release``.

    peak_gripper_opening: widest finger separation seen while opening.
    terminated: True if letting go satisfied the task predicate.

class Pick(
    success: bool,
    chunks_used: int,
    max_chunks: int,
    peak_lift_m: float,
    min_gripper_opening: float,
    final_gripper_opening: float,
    terminated: bool,
    truncated: bool,
    diagnostics: dict[str, Any],
)
    Outcome of ``pi0_pick``.

    success: the VLA's lift heuristic fired (descended, then rose by
        ``lift_thresh`` with the fingers closed on something).  It is a hint,
        not proof: confirm with ``state().gripper_opening`` and the wrist image.
    chunks_used / max_chunks: VLA action chunks consumed / allowed.
    peak_lift_m: how far the gripper rose after its lowest point.
    min_gripper_opening / final_gripper_opening: finger separation statistics.
    terminated: the task predicate fired during the pick.
    diagnostics: raw threshold bookkeeping from the primitive.

class Contact(
    success: bool,
    chunks_used: int,
    max_chunks: int,
    terminated: bool,
    truncated: bool,
)
    Outcome of ``pi0_doubled``.

    success: mirrors ``terminated`` only.  For an intermediate contact skill
        (knob, drawer, door) ``False`` does not mean the contact failed;
        inspect the state or an image.

class Segment(
    found: bool,
    world_xyz: tuple[float, float, float] | None,
    score: float | None,
    box: Any,
    camera: str,
    step: int,
    overlay_artifact: str | None,
    error: str | None,
)
    Outcome of ``segment``.

    found: a mask above ``min_score`` was produced.
    world_xyz: median world coordinate of the mask (surface point, metres), or
        None when not found / no valid depth.
    score: SAM3 confidence in [0, 1] (brand nouns score ~0.05, colour+shape
        phrases ~0.7).
    box: mask bounding box as reported by SAM3, or None.
    overlay_artifact: name of the saved overlay image (``artifact()`` loads it).
    error: why nothing was found, or None.

class BackProjection(
    world_xyz: tuple[float, float, float],
    pixel: tuple[int, int],
    camera: str,
    resolution: str,
    step: int,
    image_size: tuple[int, int],
)
    Outcome of ``back_project``: the world point under one pixel.

class RegionCenter(
    center_xyz: tuple[float, float, float],
    median_xyz: tuple[float, float, float],
    n_valid: int,
    camera: str,
    step: int,
)
    Outcome of ``region_center``.

    center_xyz: midpoint of the region's world x/y extent with median z.
    median_xyz: per-axis median of the same pixels.
    n_valid: pixels that survived the depth and z-band filters.

Exceptions:
    ToolError(RuntimeError): a call was rejected or a service failed; catch it if you have a fallback.
    ValueError: an argument was invalid (e.g. a planar move over 0.30 m) - nothing was executed.
    EpisodeFinished(BaseException): the episode is over (reason: terminated | truncated | timeout | cancelled); return.

docs.title: RoboCasa365
docs.text:
Runs on RPent

RoboCasa365 runs on RPent's RoboCasa stack: RPent boots the kitchen environment and the RLDX-1 VLA, and every robo call goes through RPent's toolkit. New robots are added through XPolicyLab (Adding a Robot).

RoboCasa365 is a household benchmark of kitchen scenes. The robot is a mobile manipulator: a mobile base and an arm, with navigation, scripted arm motions and the frozen RLDX-1 VLA.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Robot PandaOmron mobile manipulator in RoboCasa's kitchens (MuJoCo / robosuite) Action models RLDX-1 (rldx_skill, rldx_arm) Agent runtimes codex (default), claude, openai (Agent Configuration) Tasks The Target50 set: 18 atomic and 32 composite tasks Hardware Linux, NVIDIA GPU, EGL; Python 3.10 (RLDX-1 requires it)

docs.title: Observation and Action
docs.text: Item Description Observation The agentview, navview and wrist images (256 × 256), their depth and per-pixel world coordinates, and the state of the base, the arm and the episode. Action The agent's cells call robo; each call is one RPent tool (navigation, a base or arm motion, a gripper command, an RLDX-1 skill) that steps the simulator. Success RoboCasa's own task predicate. robo.done turns true once it fires, and every further motion is refused; success_criteria() returns the predicate's source, as RPent's agent can read it too. Task prompt The task instruction, a task card (the step-0 images and the robot's initial pose) and the robot's knowledge text.

docs.title: Installation and Resources
docs.text:
RPent at commit 886b3b2, in its own environment with Python 3.10 (RLDX-1 requires it) and the same torch build as for LIBERO-PRO, with PyRUA-Lean in the same environment. RPent's [robocasa] extra follows three moving branches; install .[rlinf] and those three sources at the commits the paper used instead, with the Target50 constraints (RPent's pyproject allows pre-releases):

uv pip install -e ".[rlinf]" \
    "rpent-robocasa365 @ git+https://github.com/RLinf/robocasa.git@2692d8fc5fd86708a1b2028dcbce892ec418a9e7" \
    "rlinf-rldx @ git+https://github.com/RLinf/RLDX-1.git@ebcfd13df5177e4b3e574bdf5a3b427c7c4a1e8a" \
    "robosuite @ git+https://github.com/RLinf/robosuite.git@97cfbde4b68d8ec43dad20cf4747297866a6ca2e" \
    --constraint robots/robocasa/eval/target50-constraints.txt --prerelease=if-necessary-or-explicit
uv pip install -e /path/to/PyRUA-Lean
robocasa-download-assets --assets-path /path/to/robocasa-assets --no-macros      # 23 GB

The environment (both servers pin their GPU from --cuda-device, so leave CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES unset):

export ROBOCASA_ASSETS_PATH=/path/to/robocasa-assets
export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1 MUJOCO_GL=egl PYOPENGL_PLATFORM=egl ROBOT_PLATFORM=ROBOCASA NO_ALBUMENTATIONS_UPDATE=1
export RLDX_MAX_CHUNKS=40 RLDX_SETTLE_PATIENCE=999 RLDX_ACTION_STEPS_PER_CHUNK=8     # the Target50 execution values
unset RLDX_RESET_SEED RLDX_ALLOW_RESET CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES

Reproducible scenes

Unpatched, RoboCasa can build a different scene for the same task and seed from run to run. Patch the installed file once (idempotent):

sed -i 's/list(set(valid_geoms))/list(dict.fromkeys(valid_geoms))/' \
    "$(python -c 'import importlib.util as u, pathlib as p; print(p.Path(u.find_spec("robocasa").origin).parent / "models/fixtures/counter.py")')"

PyRUA-Lean also starts the env server with PYTHONHASHSEED=0.

docs.title: VLA Configuration
docs.text:
RLDX-1 at a fixed revision, and the support files (no weights) of its backbone in the Hugging Face cache, at a fixed revision and once more at main (RLDX resolves the backbone at main; without refs/main in the cache the VLA server spends its whole boot budget retrying the Hub):

hf download RLWRLD/RLDX-1-FT-RC365 --revision 587e9ecdcc5e7184fcc17f58713908edff5af041 --local-dir /path/to/rldx
export RLDX_MODEL_PATH=/path/to/rldx
hf download RLWRLD/RLDX-1-VLM --revision 4b9f870d1287e0d38d7eb1445e6d8c60afe66dd7 \
    --include '*.json' '*.txt' '*.jinja' '*.md' '*.png' '.gitattributes'
hf download RLWRLD/RLDX-1-VLM --include '*.json' '*.txt' '*.jinja' '*.md' '*.png' '.gitattributes'

docs.title: Task Selection
docs.text: Option Meaning --task A RoboCasa365 task name, e.g. OpenDrawer. --suite The data split (default target, the Target50 evaluation setting). --seed The scene seed: 1-10 for atomic tasks, 1-5 for composite ones. Always pass it: pyrualean play sends 0 when it is left out.

docs.title: Run a Task
docs.text:
export RPENT_ROOT=/path/to/rpent
pyrualean play --robot robocasa --arm cells --task OpenDrawer --suite target --seed 1 \
    --model gpt-6-astra --max-turns 40 --budget-s 7200 --out runs/robocasa-demo --cuda-device 0
pyrualean summarize runs/robocasa-demo

An episode boots private env and VLA servers (~3 GB + ~15-17 GB of GPU memory); --vla-endpoint attaches it to a running RLDX-1 server instead.

docs.title: View Results
docs.text: The run directory keeps the episode video (episode.mp4), every cell the agent ran (workspace/) and what each printed (the runtime's event file, e.g. codex_events.jsonl), the ledger of primitive calls (calls.jsonl), the token usage and RoboCasa's verdict (result.json), and RPent's own records (states.json, per-step images and world maps).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
GPT-6 Astra, five seeds per task; at most 40 LLM calls on atomic tasks and 100 on composite ones, and two hours per episode. Against RPent's tool-calling agent with the same planner and primitives; LLM calls, input tokens and cost per solved episode on the instances both solved:

Success (%) LLM calls Input tokens Cost Atomic (90 task instances), tool calling (RPent) 78.9 10.4 261k $0.62 Atomic, PyRUA-Lean 86.7 5.6 171k $0.54 Composite (160 task instances), tool calling (RPent) 34.4 28.4 1.22M $2.01 Composite, PyRUA-Lean 39.4 14.9 603k $1.25

docs.title: What Runs Where
docs.text:
• Env server (RPent) owns the RoboCasa kitchen environment and its EGL rendering.
  • RLDX-1 server (RPent) holds the VLA.
  • PyRUA-Lean boots them for the episode, builds RPent's toolkit and serves the agent's cells against robo.
  • Agent runtime (Codex CLI, Claude Code or the openai loop) talks to the model.

docs.title: Primitives the Agent Can Call
docs.text:
Navigation and motion:

  • navigate_to(xy): drive the base towards a world (x, y) and stop facing it; move_base(forward, lateral, turn): raw base velocities.
  • move_to(xyz), move_delta(dxyz): servo the gripper to a world position or by a displacement.
  • rotate_pitch(target_pitch): tilt the wrist.
  • set_gripper(gripper, steps), release(), scripted_grasp(xyz): drive the fingers; let go; a coarse scripted grasp (open, hover, descend, close, lift).
  • rldx_skill(): let the frozen RLDX-1 VLA drive the whole body on the task instruction; rldx_arm(): the arm, with the base clamped to small motions.

Perception and state:

  • back_project_batch(pixels), query_world_map(z_min, z_max): world points under pixels, what lies inside a height band.
  • floor_overlay(): the navigation view with the floor painted.
  • state(), image(camera), depth(camera), world_map(camera), show(camera), camera_meta(camera), success_criteria(), artifact(name), done.
API reference: what the agent reads, generated from pyrualean.robocasa when these docs are built 
class RobocasaRobot
    A mobile-base PandaOmron (Franka arm with a two-finger gripper on an
    omnidirectional base) in a RoboCasa365 kitchen.

    World frame: x/y span the kitchen (coordinates run over several metres),
    z is up; metres and radians; quaternions are ``[x, y, z, w]``.
    ``state().eef_pos`` is the gripper position in this frame,
    ``state().base_pos`` the base position and ``state().base_yaw`` its
    heading.  Counters are at about z = 0.9 m; read every height from the
    world maps, never assume one.  The arm reaches about 0.8 m from the
    base: a target farther away in x/y needs ``navigate_to`` first.  Every
    base motion (``navigate_to``, ``move_base``, a VLA run) moves the arm and
    all three cameras with it, so re-localise before the next arm target.

    Gripper commands: ``robo.CLOSE`` (+1) closes and keeps squeezing,
    ``robo.OPEN`` (-1) opens, ``robo.HOLD`` (``"hold"``) servos the fingers to
    the width they had when the motion began.  ``"hold"`` is the default of
    every motion call and the carry-safe choice: a sustained +1 squeezes a
    small object out of the fingers, and carrying with -1 drops it.

    Perception is camera based: three 256x256 cameras ride on the robot,
    ``agentview`` (shoulder view: what is where), ``wrist`` (on the gripper:
    close-range geometry) and ``navview`` (forward-down floor view: where
    to drive), each with a per-pixel world map.  Object poses are never
    given.

    The frozen RLDX-1 VLA (``rldx_skill``, ``rldx_arm``) always receives the
    benchmark's own task instruction (``robo.task``); there is no prompt to
    write.  Success is the benchmark's own predicate (``state().success``,
    ``robo.done``); ``state().task_progress`` shows the values that predicate
    computes and ``success_criteria()`` its source.  Motion calls block until
    the primitive finishes and return a typed result; nothing is queued.

Constants:
    robo.OPEN = -1.0
    robo.CLOSE = 1.0
    robo.HOLD = 'hold'
    robo.MAX_MOVE_M = 0.3

Methods and attributes of `robo`:

robo.task -> str  (read-only attribute)
    The task instruction, e.g. ``"Open the left drawer."``.

    It is authoritative and the VLA acts on exactly this text.

robo.done -> bool  (read-only attribute)
    True once the benchmark's success predicate (``state().success``) has fired (sticky).

robo.state(step: int = -1) -> State
    Read the recorded state of the robot and of the episode.

    Args:
        step: recorded step to read; ``-1`` is the latest, ``0`` the
            initial scene.  A new step is recorded after every motion call.
    Returns:
        State with the gripper pose, finger positions, base pose, the
        success flag, ``task_progress`` and ``vla_desync``.

robo.image(camera: str = 'agentview', *, resolution: str = 'low', step: int = -1) -> Any
    Load a recorded camera image as a ``numpy`` uint8 array (256, 256, 3), RGB.

    Args:
        camera: ``"agentview"`` (shoulder camera: identify objects,
            fixtures and the layout; its pixels back-project directly),
            ``"wrist"`` (on the gripper: close-range geometry, best within
            20 cm of a target) or ``"navview"`` (forward-down view of the
            floor ahead of the base: where driving is possible).  All
            three move with the robot.
        resolution: there is one resolution, ``"low"`` (256x256).  Pixel
            coordinates are (row, col) with row 0 at the top and col 0 at
            the left; pass the same camera and step to
            ``back_project_batch``.
        step: recorded step, ``-1`` = latest.

robo.world_map(
    camera: str = 'agentview',
    *,
    resolution: str = 'low',
    step: int = -1,
) -> Any
    Load the per-pixel world coordinates of a recorded image.

    Returns a ``numpy`` float32 array (256, 256, 3): ``world_map[row, col]``
    is the [x, y, z] of the surface seen at that pixel (zeros where the
    camera saw no depth).  This is what ``back_project_batch`` and
    ``query_world_map`` read; load it to reason about many pixels at once
    (e.g. ``np.median(world_map[r0:r1, c0:c1, 2])`` is a surface height).
    Maps older than 25 recorded steps are deleted; a missing map raises
    ``ToolError``.

robo.show(camera: str = 'agentview') -> None
    Attach the current image of ``camera`` to the feedback of this turn.

    Images are not returned automatically; call ``show("agentview")``,
    ``show("wrist")`` or ``show("navview")`` when *you* (the author) need
    to look at the scene before writing the next turn.  Costs tokens:
    look only when a decision depends on it.

robo.artifact(name: str, *, step: int = -1) -> bytes
    Return the raw bytes of a recorded artifact (advanced).

    Names are ``agentview.png``, ``wrist.png``, ``navview.png``,
    ``navview_floor.png``, ``<camera>_world.npz`` (all three cameras),
    ``<camera>_depth.npz`` and ``<camera>_metadata.json`` (agentview and
    wrist only).

robo.depth(camera: str = 'agentview', *, step: int = -1) -> Any
    Load the metric depth of a recorded ``agentview`` or ``wrist`` image.

    Returns a ``numpy`` float32 array (256, 256) in metres.  ``navview``
    has no depth map (use its world map).

robo.floor_overlay(step: int = -1) -> Any
    Load the navview image with the floor painted green: uint8 (256, 256, 3), RGB.

    Floor = pixels whose world z lies between -0.2 and 0.12 m; green
    area ahead of the base is where it can drive.

robo.camera_meta(camera: str = 'agentview', *, step: int = -1) -> dict[str, Any]
    Return the camera calibration of a recorded step as a dict (``agentview`` / ``wrist``).

    Keys: ``intrinsic`` (3x3), ``extrinsic_cam2world`` (4x4), ``height``,
    ``width``, ``depth_near`` / ``depth_far``.  Both cameras move with the
    robot (the wrist camera with the gripper), so read the meta of the
    same step as the image.

robo.success_criteria() -> str
    Return the source code of this task's success predicate (``_check_success``).

    It names the objects and fixtures that matter and the thresholds
    (e.g. a drawer joint fraction of 0.95, a ``success_time`` counter)
    that ``state().task_progress`` reports live.  It contains no object
    coordinates.

robo.back_project_batch(
    pixels: Sequence[Sequence[int]],
    *,
    step: int = -1,
    camera: str = 'agentview',
    resolution: str = 'low',
) -> BackProjection
    Return the world [x, y, z] under image pixels of a recorded view.

    Args:
        pixels: 1 to 50 ``[row, col]`` pairs read off ``image(camera,
            step=step)`` (a single pair is accepted too).
        step: recorded step whose world map to read, ``-1`` = latest.
        camera: ``"agentview"``, ``"wrist"`` or ``"navview"``: the pixel
            coordinate space, so use the view the pixels came from.
        resolution: ``"low"`` (the only one recorded).
    Returns:
        BackProjection; ``median_xyz`` is the robust coordinate of what
        the pixels cover.  Every point is a visible SURFACE point (the
        top of an object, not its centre): sample 3-8 pixels firmly on
        the object's top surface and use the median; pixels on thin rims,
        edges, shadows or the gap to a counter hit the background.
    Raises:
        ToolError: no world map recorded for that step / camera.

robo.query_world_map(
    z_min: float = 0.85,
    z_max: float = 0.95,
    *,
    x_range: Sequence[float] | None = None,
    y_range: Sequence[float] | None = None,
    camera: str = 'agentview',
    resolution: str = 'low',
    min_cluster_size: int = 10,
) -> HeightQuery
    Find what lies inside a world-z band of the LATEST world map, as pixel clusters.

    Args:
        z_min / z_max: height band in metres.  0.85-0.95 finds objects on
            a counter; ``camera="navview"`` with 0.0-0.12 finds walkable
            floor.
        x_range / y_range: optional ``[min, max]`` world limits.
        camera: which camera's world map (``"agentview"``, ``"wrist"``,
            ``"navview"``).
        resolution: ``"low"`` (the only one recorded).
        min_cluster_size: smallest cluster reported (pixels).
    Returns:
        HeightQuery; each ``Cluster.center_xyz`` is a candidate location,
        ``sample_pixel`` a place to look in the image to identify it.
        Always reads the latest recorded step.

robo.rldx_skill(
    *,
    base_clip: float | None = None,
    max_chunks: int = 70,
    force_reset: bool = False,
    n_action_steps: int = 8,
    settle_patience: int = 999,
    settle_eps: float = 0.012,
) -> Skill
    Let the frozen RLDX-1 VLA drive the whole body (arm AND base) on the task instruction.

    The policy always receives the benchmark's own instruction
    (``robo.task``) and the three current camera images, executes
    ``n_action_steps`` env steps per chunk and stops when the task
    succeeds, when it settles or at ``max_chunks``.  It is the tool for
    grasps, re-grasps, pulling / pushing fixtures, pressing controls and
    other contact-rich motion, and it may reposition the base by itself.

    Args:
        base_clip: cap on the base velocity commands (None = full base
            motion; ``rldx_arm`` is the same skill with 0.1).
        max_chunks: action-chunk cap.  The evaluation protocol may pin it
            (and ``n_action_steps`` / ``settle_patience``) through the
            environment; ``Skill.max_chunks`` reports what applied.
        force_reset: start from a fresh frame history even after a
            previous VLA call (the runtime does this by itself whenever
            a non-VLA primitive ran in between: see
            ``state().vla_desync``).
        n_action_steps: env steps executed per predicted chunk.
        settle_patience: chunks without arm / gripper motion after which
            the run stops as ``settled``; leave the default (999 disables
            it: the VLA is expected to run until success or the cap).
        settle_eps: motion threshold of that test, metres.
    Returns:
        Skill; check ``status``, the grasp signals and ``robo.done``.
        ``cap`` means the VLA was still acting: call again (its frame
        history continues) rather than staging by hand.

robo.rldx_arm(
    *,
    base_clip: float | None = 0.1,
    max_chunks: int = 70,
    force_reset: bool = False,
    n_action_steps: int = 8,
    settle_patience: int = 999,
    settle_eps: float = 0.012,
) -> Skill
    Let the frozen RLDX-1 VLA drive the arm with the base clamped to small motions.

    Same skill and arguments as ``rldx_skill`` with ``base_clip=0.1``: the
    VLA can micro-align the gripper for a grasp or a contact but cannot
    drive away.  Use it once the base already stands at the right place;
    use ``rldx_skill`` when the VLA has to reposition the base as well.

robo.move_to(
    xyz: Sequence[float],
    gripper: float | str = 'hold',
    *,
    step_clip: float = 0.02,
    max_steps: int = 200,
    tol: float = 0.012,
) -> Move
    Servo the gripper to a world-frame position, holding its orientation.

    A closed-loop OSC servo: each env step moves the gripper at most
    ``step_clip`` towards the target until it is within ``tol`` or
    ``max_steps`` are spent.  The first arm servo after a base motion
    spends a few extra steps calibrating.

    Args:
        xyz: target gripper position [x, y, z] in metres.  One call may
            move at most 0.30 m (``ValueError`` beyond); split longer
            traversals into 2-3 waypoints at carrying height.
        gripper: ``"hold"`` (default: keep the finger width, carry-safe),
            +1 (close and keep squeezing) or -1 (open); held during the
            whole motion.
        step_clip: per-step travel cap (m): 0.02 in free space, 0.012 for
            a fine approach or a vertical retreat.
        max_steps: env step budget.
        tol: stop when within this distance (m).
    Returns:
        Move; check ``reached`` and compare ``final_eef_pos`` with the
        target: a stalled servo returns normally.

robo.move_delta(
    dxyz: Sequence[float],
    gripper: float | str = 'hold',
    *,
    step_clip: float = 0.02,
    max_steps: int = 80,
) -> Move
    Servo the gripper by a relative displacement from its current position.

    ``target = current eef_pos + dxyz`` (tolerance 0.012 m); for small
    adjustments such as a final approach or a lift.  ``|dxyz|`` may not
    exceed 0.30 m.  ``gripper`` as in ``move_to`` (default ``"hold"``).

robo.rotate_pitch(
    target_pitch: float = 0.6,
    *,
    gripper: float = 1.0,
    n: int = 12,
) -> Pitch
    Tilt the wrist by ``target_pitch`` radians (relative, about the controller's x axis).

    Pitches the gripper forward / back over ``n`` env steps while the
    position is held by the controller (it is not actively servoed:
    expect a few mm of drift).  Use it before threading the gripper into
    an opening whose front face points along world +/-y.  ``gripper`` is
    a numeric command held during the rotation (+1 keep closed, -1 open;
    ``"hold"`` is not accepted here).  Read ``state().eef_tilt``
    afterwards; the primitive reports no angle.

robo.set_gripper(gripper: float = 1.0, steps: int = 10) -> Gripper
    Hold the gripper pose and drive the fingers with ``gripper`` for ``steps`` env steps.

    ``set_gripper(+1, steps=10)`` closes (or firms a grip before a
    carry), ``set_gripper(-1)`` opens.  Numeric only: ``"hold"`` is not a
    command here.  Verify a grasp afterwards from
    ``Gripper.gripper_opening`` (clearly above 0 = something between the
    fingers) and the wrist image.

robo.release(steps: int = 10) -> Gripper
    Open the gripper in place for ``steps`` env steps (``set_gripper(-1, steps)``).

    Release only when the object is supported at its destination, then
    retreat upwards and check that it stayed put.  ``terminated``
    reports whether letting go satisfied the task.

robo.scripted_grasp(
    xyz: Sequence[float],
    *,
    approach_z: float = 0.1,
    grasp_z_offset: float = 0.0,
    step_clip: float = 0.02,
) -> Grasp
    Coarse scripted grasp: open, hover ``approach_z`` above ``xyz``, descend, close, lift.

    A fallback for simple, well-localised objects; prefer ``rldx_arm``
    for anything hard.  ``grasp_z_offset`` shifts the closing height
    (negative = below the sampled surface point); ``step_clip`` caps the
    descent speed.  The hover point must be within 0.30 m of the gripper.
    Returns Grasp; ``ok`` False names the ``stage`` that stalled.

robo.navigate_to(
    xy: Sequence[float],
    *,
    tol: float = 0.2,
    max_steps: int = 300,
    gripper: float | str = 'hold',
) -> Navigation
    Drive the base towards a world (x, y) and stop facing it.

    The base first turns to face the target, then drives forward at full
    speed (about 2.3 mm per env step, so 300 steps cover roughly 0.7 m)
    with closed-loop steering until it is within ``tol``; the first call
    spends a few steps calibrating the heading.  There is no path
    planning: choose a target with a clear line ahead (``floor_overlay``,
    ``query_world_map`` on the navview) and expect ``stuck`` when a
    fixture is in the way.  The arm is held in place and its world
    position changes with the base.

    Args:
        xy: world target [x, y] in metres (a third value is ignored).
        tol: stopping distance (m): the standoff you want in front of a
            fixture plus the object's half depth (``tol=0.6`` stops about
            0.6 m in front of the target).
        max_steps: env step budget; increase for a long drive or call
            again.
        gripper: ``"hold"`` (default, carry-safe), +1 or -1 while driving.
    Returns:
        Navigation; check ``reached`` / ``stuck`` and re-localise
        everything afterwards.

robo.move_base(
    forward: float = 0.0,
    lateral: float = 0.0,
    turn: float = 0.0,
    *,
    steps: int = 10,
    gripper: float | str = 'hold',
) -> BaseMove
    Drive the base with raw velocities in its own frame for ``steps`` env steps.

    ``forward`` (+ = ahead), ``lateral`` (+ = strafe right) and ``turn``
    (+ = rotate counter-clockwise) are clipped to [-1, 1].  For fine
    adjustments near a fixture (a short nudge, a small turn): keep
    ``forward <= 0.4``, ``turn <= 0.3`` and ``steps <= 20`` per call,
    then re-observe.  ``gripper`` as in ``navigate_to``.
    Returns BaseMove with the measured world displacement of the base.

Result types (frozen dataclasses; access fields as attributes):

class State(
    step: int,
    task: str,
    eef_pos: tuple[float, float, float],
    eef_quat: tuple[float, float, float, float],
    gripper_qpos: tuple[float, float],
    gripper_opening: float,
    base_pos: tuple[float, float, float],
    base_quat: tuple[float, float, float, float],
    success: bool,
    task_progress: dict[str, Any],
    vla_desync: bool,
    terminated: bool,
    truncated: bool,
)
    Snapshot of the robot and of the episode at one recorded step.

    step: index of the recorded step (0 = initial scene).  A new step is
        recorded after every motion call.
    task: the task instruction given by the benchmark (authoritative; the VLA
        acts on exactly this text).
    eef_pos: gripper (end-effector) position [x, y, z] in the world frame,
        metres.  This is what ``move_to`` servos and what ``back_project_batch``
        coordinates are directly comparable to.
    eef_quat: gripper orientation as a unit quaternion [x, y, z, w].
    gripper_qpos: the two finger joint positions (q0 >= 0, q1 <= 0).
    gripper_opening: finger separation proxy |q0| + |q1|: about 0.04 at the
        start (fingers half open), about 0.08 fully open, about 0.0 closed on
        nothing; a value that stays in between after closing means the
        fingers stopped on something.
    base_pos: mobile-base position [x, y, z] in the world frame, metres.
    base_quat: base orientation [x, y, z, w]; ``base_yaw`` is its heading.
    success: the benchmark's own success predicate (``_check_success``) has
        fired.  This is the only definition of success; it equals
        ``terminated`` and ``robo.done``.
    task_progress: the live values the success predicate computes (its
        counters, flags and sub-predicates, e.g. a joint fraction, a
        ``success_time`` counter, ``is_open`` flags).  The keys are
        task-specific: read them at step 0, then compare before and after an
        action to see whether the action moved the criterion.  May be empty.
    vla_desync: a non-VLA primitive ran since the last VLA call, so the next
        ``rldx_skill`` / ``rldx_arm`` starts from a fresh frame history.
    terminated: same as ``success``.
    truncated: RPent never reports a step budget for this robot (always
        False); the host's wall-clock and decision budgets end an episode.
    .base_yaw -> float: Heading of the base about world z in radians (0 = facing +x, pi/2 = facing +y).
    .eef_approach -> tuple[float, float, float]: Unit vector the fingers point along, world frame ((0, 0, -1) = straight down).
    .eef_tilt -> float: Angle between the approach axis and straight down, radians (0 = down, pi/2 = level).

class Move(
    target_xyz: tuple[float, float, float],
    final_eef_pos: tuple[float, float, float],
    final_dist_m: float,
